body: The landscape of the Faroe Islands is defined by long, wide fjords with jagged green mountains rising directly from the water. These mountains appear more imposing and greener than those in Iceland.
The Faroe Islands are almost entirely treeless, with very few naturally growing trees.
Generation 4 coverage features a black pickup truck with a front antenna, which is always blurred. This is a key differentiator from Iceland, where the truck lacks a similar antenna.
All Generation 3 coverage in the Faroe Islands was captured with a black Street View car equipped with a plain grey roof rack. This car is unique among countries with similar landscapes.
Faroese houses are typically wooden, often featuring an above-ground stone basement painted a different color. Roofs are commonly either metal or covered with grass (turf).
The Faroese language is similar to Icelandic but can be distinguished by its use of the letter Ø, whereas Icelandic uses É and Þ.
Faroese bollards are small wooden sticks, usually painted yellow, and sometimes with a red top.
Guardrails in the Faroe Islands have yellow reflectors, a feature not found on guardrails in any other northern European country.
Directional signs are yellow with a thin white border, making them identical to signs found in Iceland.
Tórshavn is the largest town and the only place with buildings taller than three floors. The landscape around it is relatively open, especially to the east.
Klaksvík, the second-largest town, is recognizable by its location in a narrow fjord with steep hills running north to south.
There are three wind parks on the Faroe Islands. The largest is northwest of Tórshavn, with smaller ones northeast of Tórshavn and east of Vestmanna.
The village of Kirkjubøur is recognizable by its many black houses with grass roofs and a small church ruin.
The trekker on Koltur island is identifiable by the view of a narrow, low peninsula on its southeastern tip.
The trekker on Eiðiskollur is characterized by the extremely low clouds that often surround the peninsula.
The trekker west of Skopun offers a view of a wide strait to the north, with the main islands visible in the background.
From the trekker on Klakkur, you can see two distinct pyramid-shaped mountains to the south, often with a thin layer of snow.
The trekker near Gjógv provides a view of the village to the south, set against a backdrop of snow-covered mountains.
A grey boat with people in reflective clothing and the text '''RIB62''' can be seen in the coverage heading towards Koltur island.
